newsitem.title: UK: Britain urges step-back from N.Irish march brink.
newsitem.headline: Britain urges step-back from N.Irish march brink.

text.p: Britain urged feuding Protestants and Catholics on Sunday not to catapult Northern Ireland into chaos during the province's hotly disputed "marching season".

Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam made an impassioned plea for rival groups to compromise about the most controversial Protestant parade, in Portadown on July 6, and pledged she would do everthing to avert a repeat of the turmoil that erupted last year.
"Some people seem determined to push Northern Ireland to the brink. We will all pay a very heavy price if they are allowed to succeed," Mowlam wrote in Belfast's Sunday Life newspaper.

Urging a redoubling of efforts to stave off trouble at the parade by the Protestant Orange Order through a Catholic enclave, Mowlam said Britain would publish new laws later this year to defuse years of controversy about annual parades.

"To the two groups involved I say, pull back from the brink. Think about the consequences of what you are planning to do for people everywhere in Northern Ireland. It is not too late. There is no shame in compromise," she said.

Mowlam has been immersed in efforts to end an impasse over controversial marches since coming into office on May 1, when Labour won a landslide victory over the ruling Conservatives. She said she was was determined that the rule of law would be upheld.
Last July the province lurched into sectarian turmoil during a confrontation over the march from Drumcree, on the edge of Portadown town, through a Catholic enclave.
Police at first banned the march to prevent trouble but did a U-turn after four days of militant Protestant demonstrations, sparking riots that brought the province to a standstill.
Catholics, who generally favour an end to British rule and union with the Irish Republic, erupted in fury when the pro-British Orangemen were allowed to proceed through the nationalist zone.

Catholics, who are in a 40-60 minority in the province, regard the parades as inflammatory and anti-Irish. The Orange Order says the Portadown march is a simple parade to celebrate their religious faith.
Hardline Protestant leader Ian Paisley called on Britain on Saturday to ensure that the Portadown parade was not routed away from the Catholic zone.
The outspoken politician-cleric made the demand after talks brokered by Mowlam on Friday failed to produce agreement.
After eight hours liaising between the Order and Catholic residents in separate rooms, she said no resolution had been found but promised to keep in touch with both sides over the coming days.
Paisley said there was only one way the controversy could be settled, and "that is by the British government establishing for all time the right of people to walk on the Queen's highway".
The Protestant marching season climaxes on July 12 in province-wide processions marking the anniversary of a landmark Protestant battlefield victory of the Catholic Irish in 1690.
